hint: It is the opposite of lesson 13's pattern.

choices.text: Sends one stream of work to several goroutines
choices.why: That is fan-out, lesson 13.

choices.text: Merges several channels into one
choices.why: Right: one loop reads whatever any input produces.

choices.text: Sorts the values of a channel by the time they were sent
choices.why: Nothing sorts; values arrive in the order they are copied across.

choices.text: Limits how many goroutines run at once
choices.why: That is the worker pool's job, lesson 7.

prompt: Why does `merge` start one copier goroutine per input instead of reading the inputs one after another in a loop?
hint: What happens to the others while one input has nothing to send?

choices.text: Goroutines copy values faster than a loop does
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; blocking is.

choices.text: A loop waiting on one quiet input would hold up the rest
choices.why: Right. Each input can block at any moment, so each needs its own goroutine to wait on it.

choices.text: Generic functions require one goroutine per argument
choices.why: Generics have nothing to do with goroutines.

choices.text: A channel can be read by only one goroutine at a time
choices.why: Lesson 13 had three workers reading one channel at once.

prompt: A colleague moves `wg.Wait()` and `close(out)` out of their goroutine, into `merge` itself just before `return out`. What happens when `main` calls `merge`?

choices.text: It works the same, one goroutine fewer
choices.why: `merge` has not returned `out` yet, so nobody can receive what the copiers send.

choices.text: `out` is closed before any value is sent
choices.why: `wg.Wait()` comes first, and it never returns.

choices.text: It never returns: the copiers block sending to a channel nobody reads
choices.why: Right. `merge` waits for copiers that wait for a reader that is waiting for `merge` to return.

choices.text: The copiers panic with `send on closed channel`
choices.why: Nothing is closed: the program is stuck before reaching `close`.

prompt: `merge.go` merged three sources: `disk` sent 3 readings, `net` 4 and `cpu` 2. How many readings did `main` print before `all sources closed`?
hint: A merge loses nothing and adds nothing.

prompt: `spin.go` counted 972,922 zero values in 100 ms although only six numbers were sent. Where did the zeros come from?
hint: What does a receive from a closed channel do?

choices.text: From the closed channels, which are always ready
choices.why: Right. A receive from a closed channel returns the zero value at once, every time.

choices.text: From `numbers`, which sends a zero after its last value as an end marker
choices.why: `numbers` sends 1 to 3 and closes; nobody sends a zero.

choices.text: From the timer, which ticks every nanosecond
choices.why: `time.After` delivers once, after 100 ms, and ends the loop.

choices.text: From the `select` picking an empty case
choices.why: There is no empty case; the two receives were simply always ready.

prompt: In `pair.go`, what does `b = nil` do once `b` has closed?
hint: Lesson 5: a nil channel in a `select`.

choices.text: It closes `b` a second time, harmlessly
choices.why: It closes nothing, and closing twice would panic.

choices.text: It frees the memory of the channel for the garbage collector straight away
choices.why: It changes the loop's variable; collection is not the point.

choices.text: Switches that case off for the rest of the loop
choices.why: Right. A nil channel is never ready, so its case is never chosen again.

choices.text: It makes the `numbers` goroutine stop sending
choices.why: That goroutine had already finished; the variable is the loop's own handle.

prompt: A program merges a list of channels whose length is known only when it runs. Which merge fits?
hint: How many `case` lines does a `select` have?

choices.text: A `select` with one case per channel
choices.why: Each case is written in the source, so the number is fixed when the code is written.

choices.text: Section 02's `merge`
choices.why: Right: one goroutine per input, however many there turn out to be.

choices.text: Reading the channels in turn in a `for` loop
choices.why: A quiet channel would hold up all the others.

choices.text: Any, since `range` works over a list of channels
choices.why: `range` over a slice gives you the channels, not their values.

prompt: To tell a closed channel from a real value, receive with the comma-ok form, `v, ___ := <-a`, which is false once `a` is closed and drained.
`early.go` closed `out` right after the first copier's loop. What did the program end with?
hint: The other copier was still sending.

choices.text: `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`
choices.why: That is `never.go`, the opposite mistake.

choices.text: `panic: send on closed channel`
choices.why: Right, at line 26, the slow copier's `out <- v`.

choices.text: Three slow readings after the fast one
choices.why: Only one slow reading arrived before the panic.

choices.text: `main is done`, after a pause
choices.why: The panic ended the program first.

prompt: `never.go` stopped with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`. Why might the same bug in a server raise no error at all?
hint: When does the runtime report a deadlock?

choices.text: Servers disable the deadlock check
choices.why: There is no switch; the check needs every goroutine blocked.

choices.text: A server closes every channel when a request ends
choices.why: Nothing closes channels on your behalf.

choices.text: Other parts of the server are still running
choices.why: Right. The stuck reader just waits for ever, a leak only a goroutine count shows.

choices.text: In a server the `range` ends after a timeout
choices.why: `range` over a channel has no timeout.

prompt: A merge has three copiers. Which code may close its output channel?
hint: The last sender closes; who knows which one is last?

choices.text: Whichever copier finishes first
choices.why: That is `early.go`: the others still send.

choices.text: Each copier, guarded by a recover
choices.why: Recovering hides a panic; the second close and the later sends are still wrong.

choices.text: `main`, after reading a fixed number of values
choices.why: A receiver closing a channel others send on is the early close again, from the other side.

choices.text: A goroutine that waits on a `WaitGroup` the copiers count down
choices.why: Right. Only something that counts them knows when all three are done.

prompt: Put the life of section 02's `merge` in order, from the call to the end of `main`'s loop.
hint: The closer starts before any value moves.
items: one copier goroutine starts per input
a goroutine starts waiting on the `WaitGroup`
every input closes and every copier calls `Done`

prompt: Match each program of this lesson with what it printed last.
Which of these merges end with every value delivered and nothing left running? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check who closes, and whether a closed case is switched off.

choices.text: Copiers plus a goroutine that closes after `wg.Wait()`
choices.why: Yes: section 02's `merge`.

choices.text: A `select` loop that sets each channel to nil when it closes
choices.why: Yes: `pair.go`.

choices.text: A `select` loop with plain receives and no exit condition
choices.why: That is `spin.go`: it spins on zeros for ever.

choices.text: Copiers that each close the output when their input ends
choices.why: That is `early.go`: a panic.

prompt: In the run of `merge.go`, `net-3` and `disk-2` both arrived at 60ms. What decided which of the two `main` printed first?
hint: Who sends on `out`, and in what order do sends complete?

choices.text: The order of the arguments to `merge`
choices.why: `disk` was the first argument and printed second.

choices.text: Which copier's send happened first
choices.why: Right. Two copiers raced to send on `out`; the merge keeps arrival order and promises nothing about ties.

choices.text: Alphabetical order of the source names
choices.why: Nothing in `merge` compares values.

choices.text: `net` has priority because it sends most
choices.why: Channels have no priorities.

prompt: A merge with `select` must handle a channel whose zero value is a legal reading, such as a temperature of 0. Which part of `pair.go` makes that safe?
hint: How does `pair.go` know a value is real rather than a closed channel's zero?

choices.text: Checking `if v == 0` as `spin.go` did
choices.why: That would throw away a real reading of 0 along with the closed channel's zeros.

choices.text: The `for a != nil || b != nil` condition
choices.why: It ends the loop; it is the `ok` that tells a value from a close.

choices.text: The `ok` of `v, ok := <-a`
choices.why: Right. `ok` is true for every value sent, zero included, and false only once the channel is closed.

choices.text: Sending values as pointers so nil marks the end
choices.why: That changes the type to work around a problem `ok` already solves.
